text: Seventeenth of August, 2026.
The BJP names a new head for its IT cell: Deepak Mhaskey.
A former chemistry professor from Chhattisgarh, who had worked on the party's IT operation there since 2009, according to Outlook.
He replaces Amit Malviya, who had run the cell for eleven years.
The party gave no public reason.
ThePrint, citing party insiders, linked the change to Gen Z protests that had exposed gaps in the party's social media outreach.
So what exactly changed hands?
To answer that, we have to rewind. Nineteen years.
2007. The BJP sets up an IT cell, under party president Rajnath Singh.
Its first head is Prodyut Bora.
Around 2010, by one account, Arvind Gupta takes over.
Then, in 2015, under the new party president Amit Shah, Amit Malviya becomes national head.
Bora, the founder, later left the BJP.
In 2018 he told reporters the cell had become, in his words, a Frankenstein's monster, and that the rot started with Team Modi.
That is his opinion, from someone who had left the party. Keep it in mind. First, the scale.
September 2018. Kota, Rajasthan. Amit Shah, then party president, speaks to the party's social media volunteers.
He describes the party's WhatsApp groups in Uttar Pradesh, with, as reported, about thirty-two lakh members.
And according to The Quint, he says: we can spread any message we want, whether it is true or false.
His example was a story about Akhilesh Yadav that he himself called untrue, and which, he said, went viral anyway.
Reports differ on whether he added a caveat that day. Months earlier, in Delhi, he had reportedly told volunteers not to post fake news.
Now, the scale, in numbers the party's own people have given.
For the 2019 general election, a cell phone pramukh was planned for each polling booth: about nine lakh volunteers, as reported.
Bihar, 2020. Party leaders told ThePrint about nine thousand five hundred IT cell heads, and seventy-two thousand planned WhatsApp groups.
Karnataka, 2023. About a hundred and fifty thousand workers on WhatsApp, a former state social media head told The Washington Post.
And in 2024, Rest of World and Princeton's Digital Witness Lab reported more than four hundred BJP-run WhatsApp groups in Mandi.
Mandi is a town of about twenty-six thousand people.
All of it runs on an app with about five hundred million users in India, according to Meta.
WhatsApp changed its own rules here. In July 2018, after lynchings linked to rumours, it limited forwarding in India to five chats at a time.
Who makes the content? Newslaundry reported a twenty-five-member core team in the Uttar Pradesh unit alone, plus about twenty designers, technicians and cartoonists.
And one number nobody can give you is the size of the whole machine. No independent body has ever measured it.
Then there's the money. And here, the paper trail is the party's own.
In its expenditure report to the Election Commission, the BJP declared spending one thousand seven hundred and thirty-seven crore rupees on the 2024 Lok Sabha election.
Six hundred and eleven crore of it went on media advertising.
About a hundred and fifty-seven crore to Google India. About twenty-five crore to Facebook.
Online, it was the campaign's biggest political advertiser, placing over half of more than two lakh Google ads.
And Election Commission data show the party's funds: seven thousand one hundred and thirteen crore rupees.
Congress: eight hundred and fifty-seven crore.
Scale and money are not wrongdoing. Every party campaigns, and every party wants reach.
The questions are about what travels through the machine.
December 2020. During the farmers' protests, Amit Malviya posts a clip of a policeman and an elderly farmer.
Twitter labels it manipulated media, reported as the first such label in India.
Fact-checkers said the clip was trimmed: a longer video showed police batons swinging at the farmer.
Twitter declined to explain why it chose that post.
In 2021, Twitter put the same label on a post by BJP spokesperson Sambit Patra. A spokesperson, not the IT cell, but the same party.
Then there's the trend machine.
In 2019, researchers joined more than six hundred public pro-BJP WhatsApp groups.
They found seventy-five coordinated campaigns to push hashtags onto Twitter's trending lists.
Their peer-reviewed paper says the organiser was most likely the party's social media arm, but they could not confirm it.
They also found the campaigns were smaller than media reports had suggested, and no evidence that anyone was paid.
Pay comes up elsewhere. In 2024, Decode reported that a consultancy working for the BJP paid young influencers for reels, unlabelled.
Asked what it pays influencers, the BJP declined to say, and pointed to rival parties doing the same.
The sharpest criticism came from inside the party.
September 2020. BJP MP Subramanian Swamy wrote: the BJP IT cell has gone rogue.
He said some members were attacking him with fake-ID tweets, and he demanded Malviya's removal.
The party kept Malviya.
Platforms faced questions too. In 2020, the Wall Street Journal reported that Facebook's top policy executive in India opposed applying hate-speech rules to a BJP politician.
Facebook said her view was not the only factor. It later banned the politician.
In 2016, journalist Swati Chaturvedi's book alleged that volunteers were handed a hit list of journalists.
The BJP's then IT head said her source had never been part of the cell, and called the claim false.
Now, the other side. Because this is not a one-party story.
April 2019. Facebook removes six hundred and eighty-seven pages and accounts it linked to the Congress IT cell, for coordinated inauthentic behaviour.
In the same announcement, it removes fifteen linked to an IT firm, Silver Touch, which, as reported, ran a pro-BJP page.
An Oxford study of that election found junk news on both sides: twenty-eight percent of links on pro-BJP pages, twenty-one percent on pro-Congress pages.
May 2024. Police arrest members of the Telangana Congress social media team over a doctored video of Amit Shah.
Congress's president responded that it was the BJP that specialised in fake videos.
And one of the biggest stories against the IT cell collapsed.
In 2022, The Wire published an investigation into an app it called Tek Fog, said to hijack trends.
Months later, The Wire took it down, and said it had been deceived by a member of its own team.
Malviya said he would sue. So Tek Fog is not evidence, and this film doesn't use it.
The BJP's own case is simple. This is organised political communication, by volunteers. The kind every party runs.
It has denied directing abuse, and says following an account is not endorsing it.
So who checks any of this?
In 2023, the government amended the IT Rules to let its own fact-check unit flag online content about its business as false.
In September 2024, the Bombay High Court struck that down as unconstitutional.
Platforms, fact-checkers, courts, rival parties. Everyone is checking someone.
Which brings us back to the seventeenth of August.
A new name at the top. The groups, the volunteers, the budget: still there.
The machine didn't change hands. It changed drivers.
And the question it leaves isn't who runs it. It's who checks what it sends.
Leaked toolkits, Newslaundry reported, have listed ready-made tweets and hashtags for supporters to post at set times.
The party's own figure, as reported, is about twelve lakh social media volunteers. That's a claim, not a measurement.
Its audited accounts for 2023 to 24 show about one thousand seven hundred and fifty-four crore rupees on election and general propaganda.
On WhatsApp, the same study classed about a third of the BJP's visual content, and over a quarter of Congress's, as divisive or conspiratorial.
